lines: A head of marketing asks for one thing: real-time, accurate revenue on the executive dashboard.
Engineering builds a streaming job to answer it. Finance keeps its own separate total. At the first board meeting, the two numbers don't agree.
Both teams genuinely met the sentence they were handed. So what did that sentence actually fail to say?
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
Real-time sounds like a claim about speed. Is the gap between these two numbers really a speed problem, one system answering slower than the other?
Or is it about something neither word ever pinned down at all: exactly what gets counted, and when a number is allowed to stop changing?
answer: It isn't speed. Neither system was slow, and neither one miscounted by its own definition.
The sentence never said whether an order counts the moment it's placed or only once it finishes settling, and it never said when a number becomes final.
That's a gap in what gets counted, not in how fast it arrives — exactly the kind of gap a fixed checklist exists to catch before anyone writes a line of code.

lines: Here's the fixed habit that catches it: five questions, asked of this exact sentence, every single time.
Who is this measured for. Where, exactly, is it measured. At what percentile. Over what window. And what happens the moment it's missed.
Answer all five for the dashboard, and real-time stops being a mood and becomes one number: a maximum staleness the dashboard is actually built to meet.
Now run the same sentence through a second checklist: six dimensions, every time, no exceptions.
Freshness and latency both come back with a real number for this ask.
Two of the six come back with nothing at all. Those two are precisely where the two teams, left to their own judgment, quietly chose differently.
Take just one of those six words — correct — and it turns out to not be one idea at all.
Run the identical dashboard ask through four separate definitions of what correct could mean here, and each one hands back a genuinely different system, with a genuinely different dominant cost.
Four systems, not four phrasings of the same system.
So which of those four does this dashboard actually need?
Look at what actually happens if the number is wrong: a board loses a little confidence in a meeting, nothing more.
That's a far cheaper consequence than a bill going out wrong, and it's the consequence — not habit, not what sounds more rigorous — that should be picking the system.
Try the identical five questions on a second ask: just make it reliable.
Who is this for. Where is it measured. At what percentile. Over what window. What happens on a miss.
Every single one comes back empty. Not vague — empty. Nobody has proposed anything to measure yet.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
Suppose the entire room spends an hour and genuinely agrees on what reliable should mean here.
Does that agreement, on its own, turn the sentence into something an engineer can actually build against?
answer: No, and this is the trap worth naming directly.
Agreeing on a word is a fact about the room, not a measurement about the system.

Until somebody names where it's measured, what number counts as meeting it, over what window, and what happens on a miss, there is still nothing to build — exactly what the five questions are there to expose.

lines: So: five questions that turn a vague word into one number. Six dimensions that make sure nothing gets silently skipped.
Correct, chosen before anything is built, from the actual cost of being wrong — not discovered afterward.
And an unmeasurable ask, rejected outright, no matter how much the room agrees on its wording.
One more, to use this for real: the warehouse must never show a customer someone else's order.
Which of the six dimensions does that sentence actually name? And given the real consequence of getting it wrong, which of the four definitions of correct does it force?
answer: That's a correctness requirement, and the consequence is a privacy incident, not a wrong total.
A privacy incident doesn't tolerate a small, bounded rate of being wrong the way a revenue dashboard does — it forces something much closer to the strict, exactly-once end of the four definitions.
Showing the wrong order isn't downtime, which is what availability actually measures; it's the system confidently handing out the wrong answer, a correctness failure with teeth.
